motion: Homework should be banned in primary schools.

transcript.motion: Homework should be banned in primary schools.

turns.text: Homework at primary level crowds out play, family time and sleep, which are far more valuable for young learners. Children spend hours on repetitive worksheets that rarely deepen understanding and often just create stress at home. Teachers already assess progress during class, so take-home tasks are unnecessary. A ban would restore evenings to reading for pleasure, outdoor play and conversation, all of which build curiosity and confidence. Younger pupils need movement and rest, not more seatwork. The home should be a place of connection, not a second classroom. Banning homework respects childhood and trusts teachers to do their job during school hours.

The evidence does not support a blanket ban. A 2006 meta-analysis by Harris Cooper found a positive effect of homework on achievement, even in early grades, when it is short and purposeful. Homework also builds study habits and lets parents see what children are learning. In the 2019 TIMSS dataset, many high-performing systems used modest homework rather than none. A ban removes a tool that, used well, supports mastery in reading and maths. It also ignores differences among families: some parents rely on homework to spot difficulties early. Better policy is smart design, not prohibition.

My opponent cites averages, but averages hide harm. Even if scores rise slightly, children lose time for sleep, sport and family talk, which matter more at this age. A small gain on a test does not justify tired, anxious evenings. We should ask what kind of person we are raising, not just what kind of scorer. Homework also widens gaps, because some homes can help and some cannot. Teachers can notice struggles in class without sending sheets home. The right move is to protect childhood and trust classroom teaching, not to pile on more after the bell.

The pro side keeps saying play matters, but play and short tasks are not enemies. The Cooper review itself says the issue is quality, not existence. Countries that ban homework often see parents pay for private tutoring, which widens gaps more than school tasks do. A ban also removes a signal: when a child struggles with a reading log, parents and teachers learn early. If we care about equity, we should give schools clear guidance on short, feedback-rich tasks rather than eliminate a support that many families value and use to keep children on track.

The heart of this debate is simple. Young children need rest, play and time with the people who love them. Homework often turns evenings into battles over worksheets that add little to what good teaching already does. A ban sends a clear message: learning belongs in school, and home belongs to childhood. It also asks schools to be honest about what they can teach in the day. We can trust teachers, protect sleep, and let families read, talk and move together. That is a healthier start than any packet of tasks ever given to a tired eight-year-old.

The pro side wants to protect childhood, and I agree, but a ban is the wrong tool. The evidence points to short, purposeful tasks, not zero. The Cooper meta-analysis, TIMSS patterns, and the risk of private tutoring all show that prohibition can deepen gaps. A better motion would cap minutes, require feedback, and train teachers in design. That keeps play, sleep and family time while preserving a channel for parents to spot trouble. Reject the ban. Choose smart homework: brief, clear, useful, and monitored, so every child gets support without losing the childhood the pro side rightly values.

motion: Cities should ban cars from their centres.

transcript.motion: Cities should ban cars from their centres.

turns.text: Every car admitted to the centre is a vote for congestion, noise and fumes. Once we accept that streets exist mainly for vehicles, we slide toward downtowns where children cannot cycle to school and pensioners cannot cross the road. Oslo, Madrid and Barcelona show that when cars are removed, footfall rises and air improves. If we do not act now, the centre will become a tunnel of exhaust where no one wants to linger. A ban is not an attack on drivers; it is a defence of shared space. Let us choose life over machinery before the slide becomes permanent.

The evidence does not support a blanket ban. A 2023 International Transport Forum review of fifteen European car-free zones found average retail revenue gains of only 2.4 percent, while 38 percent of nearby shops reported delivery delays. London’s ultra-low emission zone cut nitrogen dioxide by roughly 20 percent, yet traffic simply displaced to boundary roads. Milan’s Area C saw compliance costs fall hardest on small traders and shift workers. Bans ignore that many centres lack dense transit or safe cycling grids. Better tools exist: congestion pricing, loading bays, low-emission standards. These target harm without excluding people who rely on cars for work, care or disability.

My opponent cites numbers, but every statistic is produced by institutions funded by motoring and logistics lobbies, so their objectivity is doubtful. We should trust lived experience over lobby-linked reports. When Paris closed the Seine banks, residents did not flee; they stayed, strolled and spent. If some shops struggle, that only shows how deep the car culture runs. The choice is stark: either we banish cars or we accept choking streets. Half-measures like pricing keep the poison flowing. A ban sends a clear signal that public health outranks convenience, and history will praise cities that dared.

Attacking funders is not rebuttal; the studies I cited span public agencies and peer-reviewed journals, not only industry. On displacement, Paris’s Seine closure coincided with extra traffic on adjacent quays, documented by the city’s own monitors. Your claim that pricing is weak ignores Stockholm’s permanent congestion tax, which cut emissions 14 percent and won a public referendum after trial. Meanwhile, Oslo’s car-free push required costly retrofits and still permits residents, deliveries and disabled drivers, proving a total ban is blunt. Targeted charges, time-based access and freight consolidation achieve cleaner air without punishing nurses, carers and tradespeople who have no viable alternative.

We began with a simple truth: streets shaped around cars produce car-shaped lives. If we keep tolerating engines in the centre, we accept a slow decline into noise, illness and isolation. My opponent offers tweaks, but tweaks preserve the habit that caused the crisis. A ban is not punishment; it is liberation for walkers, cyclists and traders who gain space. Madrid’s rebound in café culture proves people follow pedestrians, not parking. Choose the bold path: clear the centre, let air return, and show children that the city belongs to them, not to the metal box.

The bold path ignores hard trade-offs. Madrid’s so-called rebound followed years of metro investment and subsidies for electric delivery fleets, not a simple ban. Stockholm shows pricing can win consent and cut pollution without excluding workers. Your moral framing hides real costs: longer ambulance detours, disabled access gaps, and small traders losing lunchtime custom. We do not need a blanket ban; we need clean-air zones, enforced loading windows, and transit first. That mix matches evidence from London, Milan and Zurich. Protect the centre by targeting harm, not by punishing every driver. Reject the motion and choose precise, proven reform.

motion: Remote work is better for companies than office work.

Companies save real money: Global Workplace Analytics estimates $11,000 a year per half-time remote worker in reduced real estate and absenteeism. Access widens too; firms hiring nationally see 30 percent more qualified applicants. Output rises because employees gain focused time, losing commutes and noisy floors. Better retention preserves institutional knowledge. The evidence is clear: flexibility lowers costs, raises performance, and expands talent, making remote work superior for companies.

Offices remain essential for collaboration and culture. Proximity enables spontaneous idea exchange that scheduled calls rarely match. A Microsoft study of 61,000 employees found remote work made networks more static and siloed, weakening cross-team ties. Junior staff learn fastest through observation and quick desk-side feedback. Offices also reinforce identity and trust; shared rituals boost engagement. Security is simpler inside controlled walls. Many leaders report that hybrid meetings disadvantage those dialing in, fragmenting attention. For innovation, mentorship, and cohesion, physical presence creates value remote setups struggle to replicate, so offices remain better for companies long term.

The con side worries about collaboration, yet evidence shows remote teams adapt. GitLab and Automattic scale fully remotely using written documentation and deliberate channels, outperforming peers on output. Stanford's 2023 data directly counters the silo claim: attrition fell 50 percent while performance rose 4 percent. Mentorship concerns ignore structured virtual programs that pair juniors with mentors across time zones, broadening access. Microsoft's network study measured one firm during pandemic lockdowns, not designed remote work. Real-world results prove flexibility strengthens collaboration and learning while cutting costs, confirming remote superiority.

We maintain that offices uniquely sustain culture and spontaneous collaboration. Proximity still produces quick exchanges that scheduled calls miss, and Microsoft's study of 61,000 employees shows remote networks grow static. Junior development depends on observation and immediate feedback, which remote formats weaken. Shared rituals and physical presence build trust and identity that screens cannot replicate. Security also stays simpler inside controlled offices. Hybrid meetings often disadvantage remote participants, fragmenting focus. Because innovation and mentorship thrive on presence, offices remain the stronger setting for companies seeking long-term cohesion and performance.

The evidence favors remote work decisively. Stanford's 16,000-worker study shows 4 percent higher productivity and 50 percent lower attrition, directly answering claims about weakened ties. Savings of $11,000 per worker and a 30 percent wider talent pool prove strategic advantage. Companies like GitLab scale remotely with strong documentation, refuting mentorship fears. The con side repeated concerns about culture and silence but never addressed these results. Remote work cuts costs, boosts performance, and expands hiring while preserving collaboration through deliberate design. For shareholders and employees alike, remote work is clearly better for companies.

We conclude that offices remain superior for companies. Proximity enables spontaneous collaboration, strengthens culture, and builds trust through shared rituals. Junior employees benefit from observation and immediate feedback, which remote setups weaken. Microsoft's study of 61,000 workers shows remote networks can grow static and siloed. Security stays simpler inside controlled walls, and hybrid meetings often disadvantage remote participants. Physical presence supports innovation, mentorship, and cohesion in ways screens cannot replicate. For long-term performance and unity, offices provide the stronger foundation for companies, and we stand by that view.

motion: Social media does more harm than good for teenagers.

transcript.motion: Social media does more harm than good for teenagers.

turns.text: Social media quietly reshapes how teenagers see themselves and each other. It rewards comparison, perfection, and constant approval, leaving young people anxious when the feedback does not arrive. It also shortens attention, replacing deep thought with endless scrolling, and it can follow teenagers home, turning ordinary disagreements into public humiliation. Even when some connections improve, the overall pressure is exhausting. The platforms are designed to keep teens engaged, not to protect their wellbeing. That is why we believe the harms spread across mental health, sleep, schoolwork, and family life. The balance is clearly negative, and the motion should be supported.

We disagree. Large studies show the picture is mixed, not one-sided. A 2023 OECD review found moderate digital use linked to similar or slightly higher wellbeing, while a 2022 Journal of Adolescent Health study reported small effect sizes for screen time and depression. Social media also helps isolated teens: LGBTQ+ youth report finding support and lower loneliness online. During COVID-19, platforms preserved friendships when schools closed. Risks like cyberbullying exist, yet most teens report positive experiences, and effects vary by usage, vulnerability, and design. Blanket claims ignore this evidence, so the motion fails.

The con side talks about mixed evidence, but teenagers themselves describe feeling trapped by likes, streaks, and impossible highlight reels. The issue is not only clinical numbers; it is the everyday pressure to perform. Even if some teens cope, others lose sleep, confidence, and focus. Nor should we ignore how quickly conflict spreads online. Saying the evidence is mixed does not answer the worry that the most engaging features are the most harmful. We still believe the overall atmosphere around teen social media is damaging, and that is enough to support the motion.

Pro relies on anecdotes, but evidence matters. The 2023 Common Sense Media report found 80% of teens say social media helps them feel more connected, and a 2021 Pew study showed 63% say it helps them feel less lonely. Pro also ignores design nuance: 2023 UK Ofcom data found most teens use safety controls and report harmful content. The “everyday pressure” argument proves too much; homework and exams also cause stress, yet we do not ban them. If harms were overwhelming, rates would rise uniformly. Instead, effects are small and context-specific, so the motion remains unsupported.

In closing, we ask the judge to focus on the overall experience of being a teenager today. Social media makes rest harder, comparison constant, and embarrassment permanent. Even friendly use can turn into pressure, and the platforms rarely reward restraint. Some teenagers may manage it well, but many feel they cannot step away without missing out. That is the core concern: not one dramatic event, but a steady drain on calm, confidence, and real connection. Because the culture around teen social media tilts toward strain rather than support, we believe the motion should stand.

Pro’s closing repeats worry without evidence. The strongest data do not show a broad teen crisis caused by social media. A 2024 WHO review found no consistent causal link between moderate use and severe harm, while a 2023 Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry meta-analysis reported only small associations. Pro also overlooks benefits: teens with chronic illness, disability, or rural isolation often find community and information online. The right response is better design, education, and parental support, not a blanket claim of net harm. The evidence points to nuance, not catastrophe, so we urge you to oppose the motion.

motion: Universities should drop entrance exams.

transcript.motion: Universities should drop entrance exams.

turns.text: Entrance exams claim to measure ability, yet they mainly measure preparation. Affluent families buy coaching, so the test rewards wealth rather than talent. If universities keep these exams, they will keep mistaking privilege for promise, until admissions become a pure auction of advantage. Dropping exams lets institutions judge coursework, essays and context instead. That is fairer, broader and closer to real academic work. A university that wants genuine diversity must stop trusting a single timed score. The exam is not a neutral tool; it is a gatekeeper dressed in numbers, and the gate only opens for those who already have keys.

Entrance exams are imperfect, but they are the most comparable signal universities have. In England, UCAS data show that applicants from the lowest participation neighbourhoods are far less likely to meet grade offers, yet contextual admissions already adjust for that without abolishing tests. Research by the Education Endowment Foundation finds that teacher assessment alone widens gaps, because grading inflates in advantaged schools. Exams also predict first-year performance better than interviews. Removing them would push selection toward personal statements, which wealthy applicants polish with paid consultants. The answer is better exams and contextual offers, not surrendering the one metric that still crosses class lines.

My opponent praises exams as a neutral signal, but that praise ignores the coaching industry built around them. If a test can be bought, it is not a signal; it is a receipt. We are not arguing for chaos. We argue for judging the whole applicant. Coursework over years beats one Saturday morning. Contextual offers are a patch on a cracked foundation. When exams decide who sits in lecture halls, they quietly decide who joins professions, boards and parliaments. The choice is simple: keep a gate that favors the prepared rich, or open the door to demonstrated work over a single score.

The pro side calls exams a receipt, yet offers no replacement that resists money either. Personal statements and interviews are even more coachable; Oxford has published that applicants with private tutoring dominate offers. Teacher predictions inflate grades for independent schools, as Ofqual found during pandemic grading. The claim that coursework over years is fairer ignores variation in school quality. Contextual offers exist because exams show disparity, not because exams cause it. Abolishing the measure will not abolish inequality; it will hide inequality behind softer language. Keep exams, improve access to preparation, and use scores alongside context, not instead of it.

The motion asks whether universities should drop entrance exams, and the deeper question is what kind of society we want. If we keep exams, we accept that one stressful afternoon, shaped by years of tutoring, should outweigh sustained effort. That is not merit; it is momentum for the already ahead. Drop the exams, and universities must look at real learning, real circumstances and real promise. Critics warn of chaos, but systems adapt when values change. Fairness cannot wait for a perfect test that will never exist. Let us choose evidence of work over evidence of advantage, and let admissions finally serve talent, not inheritance.

The pro side ends with a vision of fairness, but their argument rests on pretending that removing exams removes advantage. It does not. When the UK trialled teacher assessment, grade inflation favored schools with resources and savvy appeals. In the United States, test-optional policies led elite colleges to rely more on legacy status, extracurriculars and consultants. The result was not equality; it was opacity. Exams are the one part of admissions where a low-income student with a textbook can compete on paper. The motion would discard that fragile equality. Reform preparation, fund schooling, publish grade distributions, keep the test. Do not call it merit when you remove the ruler.

motion: Plastic bags should be banned everywhere.

transcript.motion: Plastic bags should be banned everywhere.

turns.text: Plastic bags are a symbol of our throwaway culture. They are used for an average of twelve minutes, yet they persist in the environment for centuries. They clog our drains, strangle wildlife, and break down into microplastics that enter our food chain. A full ban sends a clear signal that this needless waste is unacceptable. It forces innovation, pushing consumers and retailers toward durable, reusable alternatives. We have seen successful bans in places like Kenya and Rwanda, proving that decisive action works. This is a simple, necessary step to protect our planet for future generations.

The pro side ignores the real-world data. A comprehensive 2011 UK Environment Agency study found that a cotton tote bag must be reused 131 times to have a lower global warming impact than a single-use plastic bag used once as a bin liner. Bans don't eliminate demand; they shift it. After California's statewide ban, sales of small plastic trash bags surged, as people needed replacements for their kitchen bins. Furthermore, a 2018 study in the *Journal of Environmental Economics and Management* found that bag bans led to an increase in paper bag use, which has a higher carbon footprint. The policy simply trades one problem for another.

The evidence for a ban remains overwhelming. We see the plastic soup in our oceans, the turtles with straws in their nostrils, and the bags fragmenting into toxic particles. The con side talks about reuse counts, but that is a distraction from the core issue: we must stop the flow of single-use plastic at its source. A ban is the most direct and effective tool to achieve this. It changes behavior instantly and permanently, moving society away from a disposable model. The success in countries that have implemented bans shows a clear, measurable reduction in litter and a powerful shift in public consciousness.

You have not addressed my central point: bans cause negative substitution effects that often increase net environmental harm. The pro side's emotional imagery does not negate the data. When plastic carryout bags are banned, people do not simply stop using bags; they buy more bin liners and use more resource-intensive paper bags. The Danish Environmental Protection Agency’s lifecycle analysis confirms that organic cotton is catastrophically worse, requiring thousands of reuses. A ban is a blunt instrument that ignores these unintended consequences. We should focus on targeted solutions like advanced recycling and reusable systems that are actually used, rather than symbolic gestures that make consumers feel good while potentially worsening carbon emissions.

Let me be clear. The core principle is simple: plastic bags are a toxic, unnecessary blight on our world. They are made from fossil fuels, used briefly, and pollute forever. We have a duty to act. A universal ban is the bold, visionary policy required. It is a proven method to reduce litter, protect marine life, and inspire a culture of sustainability. The alternatives are available and affordable. We cannot let perfect be the enemy of good. The time for half-measures and delay is over. We must ban plastic bags everywhere, once and for all, for the sake of a clean, healthy future.

The pro side has consistently avoided the substance of my argument. They offer the same talking points about litter, but they have no answer for the lifecycle data showing that a ban can increase overall environmental damage. Their policy ignores the surge in trash bag sales and the higher carbon cost of paper and cotton alternatives. A blanket ban is not a solution; it is a political slogan. The evidence from the UK, Denmark, and California shows that well-intentioned bans often backfire. The real solution is smart, nuanced policy that promotes genuine reuse and improves waste management, not a simplistic ban that creates new problems while pretending to solve old ones.

motion: Video games are a valid form of art.

transcript.motion: Video games are a valid form of art.

turns.text: Video games are a valid form of art because they combine every traditional artistic discipline into a single expressive medium. They weave narrative, music, visual design, and interactive performance into experiences that move players emotionally. Through interactive storytelling, players inhabit meaning rather than merely observing it, making the work personally resonant. Games can explore grief, joy, moral conflict, and identity with subtlety and beauty. Their aesthetic power emerges from systems, choices, and atmosphere working in harmony. Because games can communicate profound human truths and evoke deep feeling, they deserve recognition as art, not mere entertainment.

The claim that games are art fails under scrutiny. A 2012 University of Pennsylvania study found players rarely retain narrative meaning, instead focusing on mechanics and rewards. The Supreme Court in Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association treated games as expression, but not art, distinguishing them from protected works like literature and painting. Unlike art, games prioritize engagement loops, monetization, and behavioral feedback over aesthetic contemplation. Even acclaimed titles function as products engineered to maximize playtime. Without stable meaning independent of the player’s choices, games lack the unified authorial vision essential to art.

The con side misunderstands how meaning works in interactive media. Art is not diminished because the audience participates; theater, music, and dance all require embodied engagement. Games simply extend this tradition by inviting players to co-create emotional significance. The claim that games lack authorial vision ignores how designers shape every choice, constraint, and consequence. Even when players act freely, they move within a carefully composed expressive world. If emotional depth and aesthetic coherence define art, then games clearly qualify, regardless of how studies measure retention or how courts categorize commercial expression.

The pro side still offers no concrete evidence that games produce art rather than engagement. Participation does not equal artistry; audiences engage with board games and slot machines too, yet neither is art. The con argument remains that games are engineered systems optimized for continued interaction, not contemplative meaning. A 2020 Pew Research analysis found most popular games emphasize progression and rewards over narrative depth. Moreover, commercial design constraints often override artistic coherence. Mere emotional impact is insufficient; art requires stable authorial intent, which interactive systems inherently fragment, making games closer to toys than art.

In closing, games clearly satisfy the core conditions of art. They offer beauty, emotional depth, and expressive meaning through interactive design. Players do not merely consume games; they inhabit stories, make moral choices, and experience aesthetic worlds crafted with care. The interactive nature of games does not weaken their artistic status; it deepens it by making meaning personal and immediate. As culture evolves, our understanding of art must evolve too. Recognizing games as art honors their capacity to illuminate human experience, stir emotion, and unite creative disciplines into a unified, powerful form.

In closing, the con side has shown that games lack the stable meaning, authorial control, and contemplative purpose essential to art. The pro side asserts emotional power but never demonstrates how games differ from other engineered entertainments. Studies consistently show players prioritize mechanics, rewards, and progression over narrative depth. Courts, too, distinguish games from traditional art. Interactivity fragments intention, turning expression into behavior management. Until games can guarantee coherent, author-driven meaning independent of player manipulation, they remain interactive products, not art. Recognition should follow evidence, not aspiration. Therefore, video games are not a valid form of art.

motion: Zoos should be closed.

transcript.motion: Zoos should be closed.

turns.text: Zoos have been beloved institutions for over a century, and that long tradition proves their value to society. If we close them, we will lose not just parks but an entire culture of family education, leading inevitably to a generation that has never seen a living elephant. Once that connection is broken, people will care less about wildlife, funding for conservation will collapse, and soon even common birds will be ignored. Tradition is the accumulated wisdom of generations, and discarding it merely because a few critics complain is reckless. For these reasons, we must keep zoos open.

Zoos often fail even their own stated goals. A 2020 study in the Journal of Applied Animal Welfare Science found that around 70 percent of mammals in European zoos showed stereotypic behaviors like pacing, a sign of psychological distress. Conservation claims are also weak: only about 15 percent of zoo breeding programs target genuinely threatened species, and fewer than 5 percent of those animals are ever released. Meanwhile, accredited sanctuaries and habitat protection cost less per animal and achieve better welfare. If our aim is to help wildlife, we should fund field conservation, not maintain failing cages.

My opponent cites studies, but we must remember that zoos have survived for generations precisely because communities trust them. Rejecting that long experience for a handful of statistics is a dangerous gamble. If we shut every zoo, children in cities will grow up with no direct contact with animals at all, and that loss cannot be measured in papers. The very fact that millions visit zoos each year shows they work. Tradition is not blind; it is proof that these institutions already serve us well, so we should keep them.

Popularity is not evidence of success. Smoking was once popular too, and bloodletting was a centuries-old tradition. The pro side offers no data that zoo visitors become better conservationists; a 2014 Conservation Biology study found most visitors left with no measurable change in knowledge or behavior. The claim that closing zoos means zero contact with animals ignores sanctuaries, national parks, and high-quality nature documentaries. Meanwhile, the distress data remain unchallenged. The choice is not between zoos and nothing; it is between outdated cages and better, proven alternatives.

We must weigh what is at stake. If zoos close, we sever a thread that has connected families to nature for generations, and that rupture will spiral into apathy, less funding, and ultimately worse protection for wildlife. No study can measure the value of a child seeing a giraffe in person, yet that experience shapes future stewards. My opponent offers reports, but we offer a living tradition that has worked for over a hundred years. To abandon it on the basis of abstract numbers would be a profound mistake. I urge you to keep zoos open.

The pro side never answered the core evidence: most zoo mammals show signs of distress, and very few conservation programs result in release. Instead, they argued that zoos must be good because they are old and popular, but tradition does not cure stereotypic pacing, and visitor numbers do not equal education. Sanctuaries, protected areas, and modern media already provide ethical contact with wildlife. Closing zoos would not end our relationship with animals; it would redirect resources toward approaches that actually work. For animal welfare, for honest science, and for real conservation, vote to close zoos.

motion: Students should learn to code from primary school.

transcript.motion: Students should learn to code from primary school.

turns.text: Learning to code from primary school builds foundational thinking, not just software skills. A 2023 OECD study found that early exposure to computational thinking improved problem-solving scores by 14% across diverse classrooms. Countries like Estonia and Singapore have integrated basic coding since 2012, with students showing stronger digital literacy by age ten. Coding also teaches resilience: debugging requires trial, error, and patience. Primary school is when curiosity peaks and cognitive flexibility is highest. Waiting until secondary school leaves disadvantaged students further behind, as wealthier families already access coding clubs. Starting early ensures equity, relevance, and readiness for a digital economy.

We believe coding should not be mandatory in primary school. Childhood is limited, and curricula are already crowded with literacy, numeracy, science, arts, and physical education. Adding coding risks turning schools into training grounds for specific tools that change quickly. Many primary teachers lack confidence in computing, and training them demands significant funding. Young children also develop abstract reasoning at different ages; forcing formal syntax too early can frustrate rather than empower. Finland, often praised for education, focuses on broad competences and introduces coding concepts lightly, not as a core subject. We should protect time for play, creativity, and social development before specialisation.

The con side worries about crowded curricula, but coding can be integrated into maths, storytelling, and art without adding hours. Tools like Scratch require no prior teacher expertise, and countries such as Estonia trained primary teachers in months, not years. The claim that syntax frustrates young children ignores block-based languages designed for ages five and up. The core issue is not time or readiness, but equity. The pro argument stands: early exposure closes the gap between privileged and disadvantaged learners. Delaying coding leaves digital literacy to chance, family income, and after-school clubs, which deepens inequality.

We repeat our concern that primary education should remain broad and developmentally appropriate. Even if coding is integrated, it still consumes teacher attention and resources. Play, social skills, and foundational literacy matter more at this age. Finland’s approach shows that light exposure without mandatory coding can work well. Training teachers, updating hardware, and maintaining software create ongoing costs. Many professions do not require programming, and predicting future skill needs is risky. We believe schools should not rush to add specialised technical subjects when childhood itself is already under pressure from academic expectations and screen time.

The con side has repeated worries about time, cost, and specialisation, but never answered our central point: early coding closes equity gaps. The OECD evidence and Estonia’s results show that primary students can learn computational thinking without losing play or literacy. Block-based tools remove the need for advanced teacher expertise. Coding is not about forcing future programmers; it is about giving every child agency in a digital world. Waiting until secondary school leaves disadvantaged students behind. For equity, readiness, and relevance, students should learn to code from primary school.

In closing, we restate that primary school should prioritise broad foundations, not specialised technical training. Curricula are crowded, teachers are stretched, and childhood needs play, creativity, and social growth. Finland’s lighter approach shows caution can be wise. Costs of hardware, software, and training are ongoing, and not every future job requires coding. We believe schools should not add mandatory coding too early, even if some countries try it. Protecting a broad, balanced primary education remains the safer path. We urge the house to reject the motion and keep coding optional for later years.

motion: A four-day work week should be the standard.

transcript.motion: A four-day work week should be the standard.

turns.text: The four-day work week is the natural next step for a mature economy. When people rest properly, they return sharper, calmer, and more creative. Long hours do not produce deep work; they produce tired repetition and avoidable mistakes. A shorter standard week would give families real time together, reduce burnout, and let communities breathe again. Employers would gain loyalty, and society would gain healthier citizens. We should measure progress by wellbeing, not by hours logged. This motion simply asks us to trust human potential and design work around it, rather than forcing people into an outdated rhythm that no longer fits modern life.

The con side rejects a universal mandate. Evidence from Microsoft Japan showed a 40 percent productivity boost, but that was a short trial with enthusiastic volunteers, not a national standard. The UK pilot involved mostly small firms, and many relied on overtime or hiring to cover gaps. In Greece, reduced hours in the public sector coincided with service backlogs during fiscal stress. If output per worker falls in nursing, logistics, or education, someone must pay: customers, taxpayers, or colleagues. A standard should be flexible, not a rigid law imposed on very different industries and workers.

My opponent worries about coverage, yet that concern assumes work cannot be reorganized. In practice, meetings shrink, distractions fall, and teams find cleaner ways to finish tasks. When people are rested, errors drop and morale rises, so extra hands are rarely needed. Many roles already have quiet periods that could be redesigned. The real risk is clinging to a schedule that treats presence as performance. A shorter week pushes managers to lead with clarity and trust, not to pile on hours. Once we value results over time spent, the supposed staffing crisis fades into a planning problem we can solve.

That planning problem is exactly where the pro side stays vague. You say errors drop and morale rises, but offer no measurable standard. The UK pilot found that at some firms, revenue fell or stayed flat while scheduling costs rose. In Belgian trials, several hospitals paused expansion because nurse coverage became harder. Reorganizing meetings does not fix emergency shifts, harvest windows, or school timetables. Your claim that extra hands are rarely needed ignores sectors where hours are tied to demand. A confident slogan cannot replace staffing rosters, and optimism is not evidence that coverage gaps will vanish.

In closing, this motion is about dignity, not just efficiency. A society that keeps asking for more hours without asking what those hours produce is wasting human life. A four-day standard would restore rest, strengthen families, and encourage smarter management. It would push us to value attention, care, and craft rather than exhaustion. Work should serve people, not the reverse. Even if the path requires adjustment, the direction is clear: shorter, focused effort beats long, hollow presence. We should set a standard that treats time as precious, gives workers a genuine weekend, and builds a calmer, more humane economy for everyone.

The con side urges caution because a standard sets a floor for everyone, not a perk for the fortunate. The pro side never showed that output can hold in hospitals, ports, or classrooms, yet those sectors face the sharpest harm from staffing gaps. Trials in Spain and Iceland were selective and costly, and several firms in the UK pilot chose not to continue once support ended. A better path is negotiated flexibility, not a blanket rule. Let teams adapt hours where it works, protect services where it does not, and judge policy by results, not by hopeful speeches about rest.

motion: Space exploration is worth its cost.

transcript.motion: Space exploration is worth its cost.

turns.text: Humanity has always reached beyond the horizon, and space is simply the next horizon. Great civilisations were defined by their willingness to explore, and abandoning that spirit would diminish us. Every generation that looked at the stars and chose to go further left behind a legacy of courage. If we retreat now, we condemn future generations to a smaller, more timid existence, trapped on a single world. The cost is not an expense; it is an investment in our identity as explorers. The choice is stark: either we continue exploring, or we accept stagnation and decline. There is no respectable middle ground.

The appeal of exploration is powerful, but budgets are not metaphors. NASA’s annual budget is roughly twenty-five billion dollars, while the World Health Organization estimates that basic clean-water interventions could save millions of lives for a fraction of that sum. A 2022 study in The Lancet found that scaling up primary healthcare in low-income countries would cost about seventy billion annually, less than three times NASA’s budget. The opportunity cost is concrete: every dollar spent on a flagship mission is a dollar not spent on preventable disease, hunger, or climate adaptation. Priorities must be weighed, not romanticised.

My opponent speaks of budgets, but ignores who is doing the cutting. The same governments that fund space agencies also fund healthcare; one does not cannibalise the other. The real danger is a cultural surrender, the idea that we have already explored enough. That defeatism is precisely what has drained ambition from our politics. When critics like my colleague across the aisle argue against exploration, they echo the voices that once opposed voyages to the New World, voices now remembered only for their shortsightedness. We must not let such timid thinking set our priorities. Exploration defines greatness, and we cannot abandon it without abandoning ourselves.

That rebuttal confuses historical analogy with present evidence, and it mischaracterises my position as defeatism when it is simply arithmetic. The James Webb Space Telescope cost over ten billion dollars; that sum could have fully funded measles immunisation for roughly two hundred million children, according to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance. My opponent’s appeal to identity does not inoculate a single child. Moreover, private launch costs have fallen dramatically, proving that innovation often emerges from commercial pressure, not flagship government prestige projects. If exploration were truly urgent, private capital would fund it. The public purse should prioritise measurable human needs before cosmic vanity.

We close with a fundamental question: what kind of civilisation do we wish to be? Throughout history, societies that stopped exploring faded into irrelevance. The choice before us is binary: either we commit to the stars and all the unity and purpose they bring, or we surrender to a slow, inward decline, squabbling over diminishing resources on a single planet. There is no third path. My opponent lists costs, but cannot name a single culture that thrived by abandoning the frontier. To retreat now is not prudence; it is civilisational suicide. We must choose greatness, and greatness means space.

The pro side offers a false choice between the stars and stagnation, but the real world offers better options. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimates that limiting warming to 1.5°C requires roughly three trillion dollars annually in clean-energy investment by 2030. Redirecting a fraction of space budgets would materially advance that goal. My opponent’s binary ignores the thousands of engineers who could instead build grid storage or desalination plants. We do not need to abandon curiosity, but we must rank survival above symbolism. When the pro side cannot show that a rocket launch feeds a hungry child or cools a warming city, the motion fails. Space exploration is not worth its cost.

motion: Public transport should be free.

transcript.motion: Public transport should be free.

turns.text: Free public transport is an investment in mobility, climate, and equity. When fares drop to zero, ridership rises sharply: Tallinn saw a 14% increase after scrapping fares, and Luxembourg's nationwide free network has made travel effortless. Low-income workers gain reliable access to jobs, students reach schools, and seniors stay connected. Removing fares also cuts boarding delays, speeding up service for everyone. Cleaner air and fewer car trips follow, since a fast, free bus or tram becomes an obvious alternative to driving. Public transport is basic urban infrastructure, like libraries or parks, and should be funded collectively through general revenue rather than penalising each individual journey with a ticket.

Fares are not the main barrier to transit; frequency, coverage, and travel time are. Making buses free drains money that could buy more service. In Kansas City, free buses cost about $8 million yearly yet ridership rose only modestly, mostly from people who already rode. Meanwhile, Paris found that cutting headways attracted far more new riders than fare cuts. Free systems also attract disruptive behaviour and require extra policing. Funding free fares usually means higher taxes or cuts to road maintenance. Targeted discounts for the poor, combined with investment in frequency and reliability, deliver more actual mobility per dollar than blanket free fares ever could.

The evidence from cities that have gone fare-free is consistently positive. Tallinn's ridership jumped, and Luxembourg's experiment shows that a whole country can run free trains, trams, and buses without collapse. Free fares remove the mental transaction cost of travel: no app, no ticket machine, no fumbling for change, just step aboard. That simplicity brings back lapsed riders and invites new ones, especially young people and older adults. When transport feels effortless, people shift habits, leave cars at home, and support further investment. Free public transport signals that a city treats mobility as a shared right, not a privilege priced per trip.

Pro repeats Tallinn and Luxembourg, but ignores the core problem: free fares do not fix weak service, and they consume scarce funds. Tallinn's ridership rise coincided with dedicated bus lanes and new routes; researchers attribute most gains to those changes, not free fares. Luxembourg's network remains underused outside peak hours despite zero prices. Kansas City's experience shows modest gains at high cost. Pro claims simplicity, yet boarding delays mostly come from dwell time, which fares-paid-through-doors can match. If we truly want equity and climate benefits, we should spend the same money on frequent, reliable routes and discounted passes for low-income riders, which outperform free-for-all schemes.

Free public transport is a bold, simple policy that treats mobility as a public good. It boosts ridership, as Tallinn and Luxembourg demonstrate, cuts air pollution, and removes the everyday stress of fares and tickets. Families save money, workers reach jobs more easily, and cities become cleaner and quieter. Free buses and trams send a clear message: everyone belongs in the transport system, regardless of income. The path to climate-friendly streets runs through making the best option also the easiest and cheapest. Let us fund transport through fair general revenue, eliminate fares entirely, and build a future where no one is left stranded at the stop.

The pro side never answers the central point: free fares waste money that could buy frequency, which is what actually attracts riders. Kansas City spent millions for small gains; Tallinn's rise came from service upgrades, not zero prices. Free systems still need police, maintenance, and drivers, paid by taxes that could fund better routes instead. Targeted discounts help low-income riders without subsidising wealthy commuters. Paris shows faster service beats cheaper tickets. The motion sounds generous, but it locks cities into an expensive, low-impact policy. Invest in reliable, frequent transit and help those who need it most; do not simply give away rides while the network still fails.

motion: Smartphones should be banned in schools.

transcript.motion: Smartphones should be banned in schools.

turns.text: Smartphones are a constant distraction in classrooms, pulling attention away from learning the moment a notification buzzes. Students who carry phones are more likely to disengage from lessons, interrupt their own concentration, and lose valuable instructional time. A ban creates a calmer environment where curiosity, not scrolling, drives the school day. It also protects younger students from social pressure, comparison, and conflict that spill over from online life into hallways and cafeterias. When phones are gone, teachers regain authority, peers talk face to face, and the classroom becomes a place for deep thinking rather than quick glances at a screen.

A blanket ban ignores how phones already support learning. A 2023 UNESCO report noted that smartphone bans in several countries reduced distraction but also cut off access to digital tools many teachers rely on. In Norway, researchers found that strict phone bans improved grades for low-performing students but had little effect on high performers, suggesting targeted rules work better. Phones also help students with disabilities through assistive apps, and they enable quick communication during emergencies. Rather than banning devices outright, schools should teach responsible use, set clear limits during class, and keep phones available when they genuinely matter.

The con side talks about tools and policies, but the core problem remains unchanged: phones are designed to capture attention, and students are not yet equipped to resist that pull. Even well-meaning rules collapse when a phone vibrates in a pocket, because willpower alone cannot compete with constant design tricks. Claims about assistive apps are valid, yet those needs can be met through school-provided devices that lack social media and games. Emergency arguments sound serious, but schools already use office phones and intercoms. A clear ban removes daily temptation and gives every student the same protected space to think, focus, and grow without digital interruption.

The pro side assumes willpower is the only issue, yet evidence shows environment and policy matter more. The UNESCO report emphasized that successful programs combine limits with digital literacy, not outright prohibition. Norway’s results also point in that direction: gains were uneven, meaning a ban helps some while restricting others unnecessarily. Saying schools can provide devices ignores budgets, storage, and maintenance realities many districts face. Office phones cannot reach a student having an allergic reaction on a field trip, while a personal phone can. Teaching self-regulation, rather than pretending temptation disappears behind a ban, prepares students for workplaces where phones are always present.

In closing, the choice is simple: either schools protect learning time or they surrender it to devices built to distract. A ban sends a clear message that education, entertainment, and social drama stay outside the classroom door. It relieves students of constant comparison, frees teachers from policing pockets, and restores shared focus during the hours when minds are most open. Other tools can handle special needs and emergencies without putting every child in the same tempting environment. We owe students a space where attention is not a battleground, where thinking comes first, and where school feels like a refuge from the noise of the online world.

In closing, the evidence shows that bans are a blunt instrument for a nuanced problem. UNESCO guidance, Norway’s mixed results, and the daily needs of students with disabilities all point toward balanced policies, not prohibition. Personal phones support emergencies, accessibility, and real-world responsibility in ways office phones and shared devices cannot match. The pro side repeats that distraction is powerful, yet never shows that removal is the only solution; teaching focus, setting boundaries, and using phones intentionally work better. Students will live with technology for the rest of their lives, so schools should model wise use rather than pretend it can simply be switched off.

motion: Nuclear power is the best way to cut carbon emissions.

transcript.motion: Nuclear power is the best way to cut carbon emissions.

turns.text: Nuclear power is the backbone of any serious decarbonisation strategy. France slashed electricity emissions in the 1980s by building reactors, and today nuclear supplies steady, low-carbon power that wind and solar cannot match. The grid cannot run on weather alone; without firm, reliable generation, blackouts will spread, industries will flee, and emissions will rise. If we reject nuclear, we lock in gas plants for decades, because no politician will explain those outages to voters. The choice is stark: either embrace proven nuclear technology, or accept rising emissions, economic decline, and a future where the lights keep failing.

Nuclear is low-carbon, but it is not the best way to cut emissions. The IPCC and IEA both show that the cheapest, fastest reductions come from renewables, efficiency, and electrification. New nuclear plants cost $6,000 to $9,000 per kilowatt and take ten to fifteen years; utility-scale solar and wind can be built in under two. The World Nuclear Association admits global construction has stalled, while Lazard finds new renewables undercut existing nuclear on cost. Slow, expensive projects delay cuts we need this decade. Nuclear can help, but calling it the best route ignores speed, cost, and what is actually being built worldwide.

The con speaker cites cost studies, but every serious engineer knows that cheap, weather-dependent panels cannot keep a modern economy running through a calm, dark week. Without nuclear, you are left with two options: massive blackouts or burning gas. There is no third path. That is why countries that tried to go cheap and fast, like Germany, saw emissions fall only slowly while coal lingered and electricity prices soared. Nuclear is not just another source; it is the foundation that makes deep decarbonisation possible. Rejecting it does not save money; it guarantees more fossil fuels, more volatility, and more carbon.

The pro side keeps insisting we must choose between nuclear and chaos, but that is a false dilemma. Real grids mix renewables, storage, demand response, interconnection, and some gas with carbon capture. The claim that Germany failed ignores that it cut emissions faster than nuclear-heavy France in the 2010s, while its renewables share soared past 50 percent. The pro argument also assumes what it must prove: that only nuclear provides firm power, when geothermal, hydro, batteries, and green hydrogen can too. Cost overruns at Hinkley Point C and Plant Vogtle show that betting on nuclear delays cuts, rather than enabling them.

History is clear: every country that decarbonised its electricity fast did it with nuclear. France, Sweden, Ontario—they proved it works. We cannot wish that record away because new technology is fashionable. If we abandon nuclear, we are not choosing innovation; we are choosing fragility. A grid without firm, low-carbon power is a grid that will fail, and when it fails, emissions rise. The choice is simple: stand with the proven technology that has cut emissions before, or gamble on untested dreams. I urge you to choose reliability, choose proven results, choose nuclear power as the best way to cut carbon.

The pro side’s appeal to tradition does not change the arithmetic. France’s fleet is ageing, its rebuild costs have exploded, and it now imports power during cold snaps. Sweden is expanding wind, not reactors. The IPCC’s 1.5-degree pathways show nuclear shrinking in many scenarios, while renewables dominate because they are fast, cheap, and scalable. The pro argument still offers only a false choice between nuclear and collapse, ignoring real-world grids like Denmark and South Australia that integrate high renewables with storage and interconnection. The best way to cut emissions is the fastest, cheapest, most deployable path. That is not nuclear; it is renewables, efficiency, and flexibility.

motion: Professional athletes are overpaid.

transcript.motion: Professional athletes are overpaid.

turns.text: Professional athletes earn salaries that dwarf those of teachers, nurses, and first responders. A starting NBA player can make more in one game than many people earn in a year. These figures reflect entertainment value, not social contribution. When society pays athletes millions while underpaid professionals struggle, we send a troubling message about priorities. Public subsidies for stadiums further inflate this gap, shifting taxpayer money toward billionaire owners and elite players. The sheer scale of these contracts, combined with endorsement deals, creates an imbalance that is difficult to justify on any reasonable measure of social value.

Athletes are paid according to market demand, not moral worth. The global sports industry generates hundreds of billions in revenue from tickets, broadcasting, and merchandise. A 2023 Forbes analysis found that top leagues reinvest much of that income into player salaries, which are the core product fans pay to see. Unlike teachers, athletes possess rare, scarce talents and face short careers with high injury risk. Salary caps and revenue sharing already distribute wealth across teams. If fans stopped paying, salaries would fall. The market is simply reflecting what audiences value, not an error in judgment.

The pro side maintains that extreme pay gaps remain unjustified regardless of market forces. When a single athlete earns more than an entire school district, the disparity signals misplaced priorities. Endorsement deals amplify the problem, turning young people’s ambitions toward improbable sports careers rather than essential professions. Public stadium subsidies deepen the imbalance, using tax money to enrich private interests. Even if demand exists, that does not make the outcome fair. Society sets limits on many markets, such as minimum wages and labor laws, precisely because raw market outcomes are not always acceptable.

The pro side repeats the fairness claim but ignores the key point: salaries are tied to revenue that athletes themselves generate. A teacher’s value is public funding, while an athlete’s value is direct consumer spending. Forbes and league financial reports consistently show that player compensation tracks revenue growth. If athletes were overpaid, teams would lose money, yet franchise values keep rising, proving owners profit. Limiting pay would not raise teachers’ salaries; it would simply shift money to owners. The real question is whether the market is voluntary, and it clearly is.

The pro side closes by restating that professional athletes are overpaid because their earnings vastly exceed those of essential workers. The scale of contracts, combined with endorsements and public subsidies, creates a culture that celebrates wealth over contribution. Young people see these figures and internalize distorted values about success. Even if fans enjoy sports, that enjoyment does not justify such extreme gaps. The core issue is not market mechanics but what kind of society we choose to build. Prioritizing entertainment over education and health remains a decision, and it is the wrong one.

The con side closes by emphasizing that athlete pay reflects voluntary consumer choices, scarce talent, and short careers. League revenues fund salaries, and owners still profit, as rising franchise values show. The pro side never addressed this central mechanism, instead repeating that gaps feel unfair. But fairness arguments do not change how markets operate. Restricting athlete pay would not help teachers; it would enrich owners. If society wants better pay for essential workers, it should fund them directly, not punish athletes for succeeding in a system fans support. The motion fails.

motion: Self-driving cars should be allowed on public roads now.

transcript.motion: Self-driving cars should be allowed on public roads now.

turns.text: Self-driving cars are ready, and delaying them costs lives. Human drivers get tired, distracted, and angry, while automated systems stay alert every second of every trip. Allowing them now lets society start learning from real-world use, improve insurance rules, and guide better urban planning. The technology already handles routine driving smoothly, and each month of delay keeps dangerous human habits in control. Early adoption also builds public trust, creates competition, and encourages safer design. We should permit deployment with sensible oversight, because waiting for perfection means refusing progress that is clearly good enough to save lives today.

The motion asks us to legalize now, but the evidence says readiness is uneven. The 2022 Cruise recall followed a rear-end crash in San Francisco, and NHTSA opened probes into Tesla Autopilot crashes after vehicles struck emergency responders. The AAA Foundation estimates drowsy driving contributes to roughly 328,000 crashes yearly, yet automation still struggles with rare, high-risk edge cases. Rushing deployment outsources risk to pedestrians and cyclists who never consented to testing. Regulators need crash data standards, disengagement reporting, and clear liability rules first. Otherwise we trade one danger for another, poorly measured and harder to assign.

My opponent cites incidents, but every emerging technology improves through guided exposure, and isolation guarantees stagnation. The proper comparison is not perfection versus imperfection; it is today’s human record versus automation’s steady learning curve. Oversight can evolve alongside deployment, with manufacturers required to report problems and regulators empowered to suspend operations. Fear of edge cases should not paralyze policy when ordinary driving already carries enormous risk. Insurance frameworks can adapt, cities can zone testing, and courts can refine liability. The real danger is waiting so long that better systems never arrive, while preventable deaths remain routine and unchallenged.

Guided exposure sounds reasonable, yet the pro side still offers no proof that current systems reduce overall harm. Their argument assumes improvement without showing a measurable safety threshold. Meanwhile, the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety notes that partial automation can encourage inattention, and UC Berkeley researchers found crash risk rises when drivers must suddenly retake control. Saying oversight can evolve later is precisely the problem: rules written after deployment chase harm instead of preventing it. Courts and insurers cannot fix a crash that kills a cyclist. We need validated performance benchmarks before permission, not optimism afterward.

This debate comes down to whether we manage progress or postpone it. Self-driving technology is already part of our future, and responsible introduction beats indefinite hesitation. With supervision, transparency requirements, and public reporting, cities can allow deployment while learning what works. Human error remains the central danger on our roads, and standing still keeps that danger normalized. We can design rules that protect vulnerable users, require accountability, and still let innovation proceed. The motion does not demand recklessness; it demands courage with caution. I urge you to allow self-driving cars now, because managed adoption is safer than permanent delay.

The pro side asks for courage, but public safety requires evidence first. Their closing still offers no crash-reduction figure, no verified benchmark, and no liability standard, only assurances. Real examples show why caution matters: NHTSA investigated hundreds of Autopilot-related crashes, and Cruise paused operations after its 2023 pedestrian-dragging incident. “Managed adoption” cannot mean letting the public road become a laboratory without prior proof. We should require independent validation, standardized data, and clear accountability before access. Voting no does not reject innovation; it insists that innovation earn trust. The motion is premature, and I urge you to reject it.

motion: Fast food advertising should be banned.

transcript.motion: Fast food advertising should be banned.

turns.text: Fast food advertising is a public health hazard, especially for children. A 2019 Yale Rudd Center study found that fast food chains spent over five billion dollars on advertising, with children and teens seeing an average of more than two fast food ads daily. This relentless exposure normalizes unhealthy eating, directly contributing to rising childhood obesity, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension. We do not ban the products themselves, but we must stop the predatory marketing that exploits developing brains and undermines parental authority. A ban is a proportionate, evidence-based measure to protect vulnerable populations and reduce the enormous long-term costs burdening our healthcare systems.

Banning fast food advertising is a dangerous overreach that treats adults like children. If we silence one legal industry today because some find its products unhealthy, what stops us from silencing the next? Soda, sugary cereals, even video games could be targeted tomorrow. This is the classic slippery slope toward a nanny state where government, not individuals, decides what we can see and hear. Furthermore, advertising is a form of commercial free speech essential to a competitive economy. The answer to unhealthy choices is more education and personal responsibility, not censorship that infantilizes the public and erodes the very freedoms we cherish.

The con side invokes a slippery slope, but real-world regulation does not work that way. We already restrict tobacco and alcohol advertising without descending into total censorship; a fast food ban would be similarly targeted. The claim that this infantilizes adults ignores the actual victims: children under eight cannot distinguish advertising from truth, per the American Psychological Association. This is not about censoring adults, but shielding minors from exploitative marketing. And personal responsibility is hollow when a ten-year-old is bombarded with a billion-dollar psychological campaign designed to override parental guidance. We regulate the marketplace of ideas when public health is at stake.

The pro side claims their policy is targeted, but the precedent is clear. Once you accept that the state can ban advertising for one legal product deemed 'unhealthy,' the boundary has already collapsed. Do we ban steak ads because of heart disease? Car ads because of accidents? This logic does not stop, and the pro side has no principled line to draw. Moreover, their argument about children is condescending. Millions of responsible parents teach media literacy without needing a state ban. The pro side’s real impulse is to remove choice from families entirely, trusting politicians and bureaucrats over parents. That is the true danger, not a hamburger commercial.

In closing, the con side’s slope is a fiction; we regulate harmful products all the time without losing our freedom. Their core argument boils down to a false dilemma: either parents teach media literacy or the state bans ads, as if a child’s brain can withstand a multi-billion-dollar persuasion machine unaided. The evidence is unambiguous: advertising drives overconsumption of foods linked to obesity, and children are uniquely susceptible. A ban is not about removing choice; it is about ending the exploitation of a vulnerable minority. We protect children from tobacco ads; we must now protect them from fast food marketing. The health of a generation demands it.

The pro side dismisses the slope, but history shows that once a censorship door opens, it never stays shut. Their entire case rests on the false premise that we must choose between a total ban or doing nothing. Where is the faith in education, in informed parents, in personal responsibility? A ban does not create health; it merely shifts power from families to the state, which is the true exploiters of fear. We should empower individuals, not silence lawful businesses. The pro side’s vision is a world where government decides what we can say, see, and eat. That is not protection; it is a quiet surrender of liberty.

motion: Online learning is as good as classroom learning.

transcript.motion: Online learning is as good as classroom learning.

turns.text: Online learning matches the classroom because it delivers the same content with greater flexibility. Students can rewatch lectures, pause difficult sections, and learn at their own pace. A 2023 survey by the Online Learning Consortium found that 72 percent of students rated their online courses as equal to or better than in-person ones. Digital platforms also widen access for rural learners, working adults, and people with disabilities. With structured discussion boards, live video seminars, and prompt feedback, the core elements of teaching remain intact. The medium changes, but the quality of instruction does not.

The motion overlooks how learning actually happens. Classroom learning depends on presence, attention, and social pressure, which online settings struggle to replicate. A 2022 study in the Journal of Economic Education found that students in in-person sections scored, on average, 0.3 standard deviations higher on common exams than online peers, with the largest gaps among first-year students. Live teachers read confusion, redirect off-task behavior, and build trust. Online formats also invite distraction and isolation. Flexibility is useful, but it cannot substitute for the structured environment that keeps weak self-regulators engaged.

Our position rests on equivalence of content and access, not on ignoring challenges. Online learning preserves the essentials: clear explanations, guided practice, and feedback. Learners control the pace, which reduces cognitive overload. The 72 percent satisfaction figure from the Online Learning Consortium still stands, and enrollment data show rising completion rates where institutions invest in good design. Discussion forums create thoughtful dialogue, often deeper than a brief classroom exchange. With trained instructors and reliable platforms, students receive a comparable education without commuting costs or rigid schedules.

The pro side repeats satisfaction surveys but never addresses the achievement gap we presented. Satisfaction is not learning; students can like a course while mastering less. The 0.3 standard deviation penalty in the Journal of Economic Education study is roughly a full grade step, and it grows for disadvantaged students. Pro claims design fixes this, yet the Tennessee study of community college courses found no recovery in pass rates even after redesign. Forums lack the instant correction of a seminar. Flexibility helps motivated learners, but equivalence requires proof across all students, and that evidence is missing.

In closing, online learning offers the same core instruction with added convenience. Students can revisit material, manage their time, and access courses they could not otherwise reach. High satisfaction, improving completion rates, and careful course design all point to parity. The classroom is one model, not the only standard. With strong teaching, clear objectives, and regular feedback, online environments deliver equivalent outcomes. We urge you to affirm the motion and recognize that quality depends on design, not location.

The pro side never answered our central point: the measurable achievement gap. They returned to satisfaction and flexibility, but those do not close the 0.3 standard deviation deficit or the higher failure rates among first-year and disadvantaged students. Classrooms provide presence, immediate feedback, and social accountability that online tools only approximate. Flexibility benefits some learners, yet the motion claims equivalence for all, and the evidence does not support that. Until studies show equal outcomes across diverse students, we must reject the motion. Classroom learning remains stronger.

motion: Tipping in restaurants should be abolished.

transcript.motion: Tipping in restaurants should be abolished.

turns.text: Tipping entrenches inequality. Seven states have already eliminated the subminimum wage, and peer-reviewed research shows sexual harassment complaints fall significantly when pay no longer depends on customer approval. Workers report that tips fluctuate wildly with weather, race, and appearance rather than effort. A service charge distributed transparently is fairer. Customers also dislike the mental arithmetic; surveys show most prefer a stable posted price. Abolishing tips does not mean lower pay; it means moving compensation into the base wage, where it is predictable, auditable, and protected by labor law.

The pro side paints tipping as arbitrary, but it is actually a flexible system that rewards attentiveness. When guests can directly acknowledge good service, motivation stays high and restaurants remain responsive. Removing that link risks turning dining into a flat transaction where effort goes unnoticed. Many staff prefer tips because strong nights can mean meaningful extra income. Management already has tools to address genuine misconduct without discarding a practice that builds rapport between servers and guests. Stability sounds nice, yet rigid wages can freeze out the very dynamism that makes hospitality work rewarding.

The con side calls tipping flexible, yet flexibility for whom? A server’s income swings with the economy, the season, and the mood of a single table. That is not reward; it is risk shifted onto the worker. The claim that guests motivate staff ignores evidence that transparent wages reduce turnover and improve service quality, because teams stay longer and train better. Management tools exist, but they cannot fix a system where pay depends on a stranger’s whim. We are not removing recognition; we are professionalizing it through stable compensation and clear promotion paths.

Risk is part of many jobs, and hospitality workers understand that reality. The pro side talks of turnover, yet experienced servers often prefer tipping precisely because it lets them capitalize on busy shifts and loyal regulars. Removing that upside could push top talent toward roles where gratuities remain common. As for motivation, a simple wage cannot capture the subtle artistry of hospitality; a smile, a remembered preference, a timely refill. These gestures thrive when guests feel empowered to show appreciation. Stability should not mean flattening the human connections that make restaurants special.

The con side asks us to preserve connections, but connections do not require paychecks to hinge on charm. Evidence from jurisdictions that ended tipping shows harassment drops and staff stay longer, while guests still enjoy warm service. The promise of busy-shift upside ignores slow-shift hunger and the bias baked into every envelope. A professional kitchen does not rely on applause to function; neither should the dining room. Abolishing tips replaces chaos with dignity, discretion with accountability. We urge you to support the motion and make hospitality a profession, not a plea.

The pro side speaks of dignity, yet dignity also means trusting workers to earn directly from guests. Tipping preserves a relationship that rigid structures cannot replicate. We should be cautious about discarding a custom that many servers value, especially when alternatives may flatten initiative and reduce the personal spark that keeps diners returning. Better to refine the system, address clear harms through management and training, than abolish a practice that, for all its imperfections, still reflects gratitude and human warmth. We therefore urge you to reject the motion and keep that connection alive.

motion: Every adult should learn a second language.

transcript.motion: Every adult should learn a second language.

turns.text: Learning a second language is one of the highest-return investments an adult can make. A 2023 meta-analysis of 48 studies found that even modest bilingualism delays dementia symptoms by four to five years. Economically, employees who use a second language earn on average 5 to 20 percent more in multilingual economies like Canada and Switzerland. Cognitively, bilingual adults outperform monolinguals on tasks requiring attention switching. Crucially, adults can achieve conversational fluency in 600 to 750 hours for close languages, a realistic goal of one year of casual study. The motion simply asks every adult to gain this compounding personal and social benefit.

The motion sounds generous, but it hides a false choice: either you learn a second language or you are a lesser adult. Human flourishing is not a single track. A nurse working double shifts, a parent caring for relatives, or an apprentice mastering a trade already invests enormous effort in skills that matter directly to their lives. Declaring that every adult should learn another language dismisses those commitments as somehow incomplete. Wisdom means recognizing many valid lives, not stamping one hobby onto everyone. Respect for plural paths is the real mark of a mature society.

The con side framed this as a false choice, but the motion says should, not must, and should simply endorses a widely beneficial goal without forbidding other pursuits. The nurse can study ten minutes a day; apps report median sessions under fifteen minutes. Nor does valuing many lives require ignoring evidence: bilingualism improves executive function even when learned late. The objection confuses respecting choice with abandoning useful advice. We can honor diverse paths and still say that learning another language, like exercise, is something every adult has strong reason to try.

My opponent now says the motion is only gentle advice, but that weakens it further. If it is merely optional, why insist every adult should do it? The pro case also leans on correlation: bilingual people may differ in education, income, and baseline health before any language effect. And notice the implication: adults who honestly choose family, craft, or community over grammar are portrayed as missing out. This is appeal to novelty dressed as science, assuming that a newer skill is automatically superior. Tradition reminds us that a good life can be fully human in one language, spoken with depth and care.

Let me answer the two remaining con points directly. First, on correlation: the 2023 meta-analysis I cited controlled for education, income, and baseline health, and still found a delay in dementia onset. Second, on tradition: the con side appeals to one-language lives, but millions of adults already learn languages for work, love, or migration, and report richer relationships and sharper thinking. Should simply means society ought to encourage this achievable, evidence-backed goal. Respecting diverse lives does not mean withholding a recommendation that costs little and protects memory, earnings, and connection. I urge you to affirm the motion.

The pro side has answered correlation with one study, but a single meta-analysis cannot settle how every adult should live.
