The approach is transparent, easy to explain, and consistent with existing charges for museums and parks. With exemptions for residents and children, it remains fair. Ultimately, cities that plan for sustainability protect culture, quality of life, and long-term appeal, ensuring tourism supports communities rather than straining them.

In closing, the pro side still has not answered the central point: fees do not fix housing, transit, or enforcement gaps. Venice’s trial showed limited deterrence and high costs, so crowding persists while budget travelers pay more. The pro plan repeats general benefits but ignores evidence that rentals and policy failures drive pressure. We need targeted measures: regulate short-term lets, expand transit, and protect workers’ hours. These steps address root causes without punishing visitors or shrinking local income. A city fee is a blunt instrument that adds bureaucracy, harms small businesses, and fails to deliver what residents actually need.

motion: Group projects should not be graded in schools.

transcript.motion: Group projects should not be graded in schools.

turns.text: We believe group projects should not be graded because grades measure individual learning, yet group work hides it. A 2019 study from Stanford found that in 70 percent of graded group tasks, stronger students carried most of the work while weaker students free rode. Teachers cannot see who actually learned. This punishes diligent students and rewards disengagement. Removing grades turns group work into genuine practice, lowers anxiety, and lets teachers focus on feedback instead of scores. Learning should be visible in the person, not buried inside a team average.

We strongly disagree. Group projects teach collaboration, communication and shared responsibility, which are essential skills for modern life. Grading them signals that teamwork matters and motivates students to contribute. Without grades, many learners would simply disengage, and the project would lose structure and purpose. Teachers can design clear roles and expectations so fairness improves over time. In our view, the benefits of graded group work for social development and classroom culture clearly outweigh the concerns raised by the opposing side.

The con side says grading motivates contribution, but motivation built on points is fragile and often unfair. When one student does most of the work, the grade stops reflecting learning and starts rewarding endurance. They mention roles, yet roles do not stop free riding or reveal understanding. They also claim teamwork skills improve, but without evidence we cannot know whether graded groups actually build those skills better than ungraded practice. Removing grades keeps collaboration while protecting individual accountability.

The pro side assumes grades are the problem, but the real issue is design, not assessment. Teachers can adjust weighting, use reflections, and observe participation to improve fairness over time. Teamwork is not fragile; students learn to rely on each other precisely because there is shared accountability. Removing grades may lower effort and make outcomes harder to judge. In our view, keeping a grade while refining the process is more balanced than abandoning assessment altogether, which risks sending the message that collaboration does not matter.

To close, the con side offered no specific proof that graded groups improve fairness or learning, only hopes about design and observation. Meanwhile, evidence shows grades in group work often mask effort and understanding. We are not against collaboration; we are against attaching scores that misrepresent students. Ungraded group projects still build teamwork, lower stress, and let teachers give honest feedback. The motion protects individual accountability while keeping cooperation alive. For these reasons, we urge you to support removing grades from group projects in schools.

In closing, we maintain that graded group projects prepare students for real life, where shared work carries shared stakes. Grades encourage commitment and help teachers guide diverse learners. Problems with fairness can be reduced through better planning, communication and reflection, not by removing assessment entirely. The pro side questions motivation, yet teamwork without any evaluation may feel optional and weak. We believe the classroom culture, responsibility and social skills gained through graded collaboration are valuable. Therefore, we respectfully urge you to reject the motion and keep group projects graded.

motion: Museums should be free to enter.

transcript.motion: Museums should be free to enter.

turns.text: Museums are the memory palaces of our civilisation, and charging admission betrays their very purpose. Once we accept that culture belongs only to those who can pay, we set off down a road where every public treasure is fenced off: first galleries, then archives, then libraries, until the shared inheritance of humanity is locked away for the wealthy. The great museums were founded on the promise of openness, and that promise dies the moment a ticket booth appears. Free entry is not a perk; it is the minimum condition for a museum to deserve public funding at all.

The claim that free entry helps the public collapses under evidence. When the British Museum scrapped charges in 2001, attendance surged, but the proportion of visitors from lower-income groups barely moved, according to the Department for Culture, Media and Sport. Meanwhile, the loss of ticket revenue forced cuts to conservation and outreach. The Smithsonian, often cited as a model, relies on a $1.2 billion federal subsidy that most cities cannot replicate. Charging fees lets museums maintain collections, fund school programmes, and keep cafés and shops honest. The real enemy of access is not the ticket price but poor transport, rigid hours, and unwelcoming spaces.

My opponent cites statistics, but behind those numbers stands a simple truth: a fee is a gate, and gates exclude. The British Museum study she praises measured who walked through the door, not who stayed away because they could not afford the train plus the ticket. And the Smithsonian argument is a perfect example of why we must go further: if public will exists, funding follows. The choice is not between fees and ruin; it is between a museum that serves everyone and one that serves only the comfortable. To charge is to declare that some citizens matter more than others.

The pro side asks us to ignore trade-offs, but trade-offs are real. When New York's Metropolitan Museum moved to a recommended fee in 2018, it gained $3 million a year for education programmes serving 200,000 students, many from low-income families. The pro argument that fees are simply gates overlooks the fact that free museums often rely on donations from the very wealthy they claim to challenge. And the slippery slope about libraries and archives is just fear-mongering: public libraries in the UK remain free despite museums charging. A fee is not a moral failing; it is a tool, and like any tool it must be judged by results, not slogans.

Let me return to first principles. A museum that charges is a museum that has chosen its audience. The pro side does not need to prove that every visitor is poor; we need only recognise that the moment a price is set, a line is drawn between those who belong and those who do not. That is the logical end of the argument my opponents make: a world where culture is rationed by income. Free entry is the only policy consistent with the idea that museums are public trusts, not private clubs. To charge is to betray the very reason these institutions exist.

The pro side has offered a moral slogan, not a policy. Free entry does not magically create access; it simply shifts costs from visitors to budgets, and budgets are finite. The evidence from London, New York, and elsewhere shows that fees, when paired with waivers and subsidised transport, reach more people than blanket free entry ever has. The pro side never answered the conservation crisis, the cuts to school programmes, or the reliance on wealthy donors. A museum that is free but broken, underfunded, and empty of context serves no one. The motion sounds noble but delivers little. We urge you to vote against it.

motion: Working from cafes should be discouraged by cafe owners.

transcript.motion: Working from cafes should be discouraged by cafe owners.

turns.text: Cafe owners should discourage remote workers because laptop users depress revenue during peak hours. A 2023 National Cafe Association survey found that tables occupied by laptop workers turn over only once per shift, while dining parties turn over three times, cutting potential sales by up to 40 percent. These customers also monopolize outlets and Wi-Fi, crowding out paying diners. Discouraging long stays is not rudeness; it is rational capacity management. Owners can signal polite time limits, preserving the cafe as a place for genuine hospitality rather than an unpaid coworking space subsidized by the business.

Remote workers are valuable customers who visit frequently, order steadily, and avoid the chaos of large groups. Many cafes, especially quieter neighborhood ones, thrive on this reliable weekday traffic when tourist traffic dips. A warm laptop user often buys coffee, pastries, and lunch, adding up over hours. Discouraging them risks alienating loyal patrons and creating an unwelcoming atmosphere. Cafes are community spaces, and flexible seating supports freelancers, students, and small startups. Rather than policing customers, owners can offer designated work zones, keeping everyone satisfied and revenues healthy.

The con side calls remote workers loyal, yet loyalty measured in hours, not spending, hurts. Our earlier data showed laptop tables generate up to 40 percent less revenue per shift because turnover collapses. Even if a worker buys several drinks, they block three dining parties who would each spend more. The con side offers no response to that lost-opportunity problem. Work zones sound nice, but during peak hours every seat has an opportunity cost. A cafe that ignores turnover math will slowly lose the ability to pay rent, staff, and beans.

We maintain that remote workers bring steady, predictable income and a calm atmosphere. They arrive on weekdays, spread demand, and often become regulars who recommend the cafe to friends. Many owners report that laptop customers anchor slower afternoons and fill gaps between rushes. Creating a welcoming environment builds loyalty and word-of-mouth marketing, which no signage can replace. Rather than discouraging guests, cafes can gently encourage balanced usage. The real goal is a thriving neighborhood hub, and flexible, friendly policies help achieve that without turning a cafe into a rigid, transactional space.

The core issue remains unaddressed: prolonged laptop occupancy slashes turnover and revenue, especially at peak times, by as much as 40 percent. The con side repeats that remote workers are loyal and calm, but loyalty does not pay rent if seats are frozen. A single two-dollar coffee occupying a four-seat table for four hours is a net loss. Owners should politely discourage extended stays, using time limits or outlet policies, so cafes remain viable businesses. Hospitality means serving many guests well, not subsidizing a few. We urge affirmation of the motion.

In closing, remote workers are steady, friendly customers who support cafes through long visits and repeated purchases. They create community, fill quiet hours, and give cafes their distinctive warmth. Many owners already balance needs with informal flexibility, and heavy-handed discouragement could damage trust and reputation. A cafe that welcomes laptops signals openness, attracting diverse patrons and word-of-mouth loyalty. We believe the best policy is gentle guidance, not discouragement. Cafes thrive when they adapt, offer options, and treat customers with respect. For these reasons, we urge you to reject the motion and keep cafes welcoming for all.

motion: Electric scooters should be banned from pavements.

transcript.motion: Electric scooters should be banned from pavements.

turns.text: Pavement riding creates unacceptable risk. In London, e-scooter collisions involving pedestrians rose sharply after rental schemes launched, and several hospital trusts reported fractures among older people and children. Pavements are designed for walking speeds, not vehicles travelling fifteen miles per hour. A scooter weighs much more than a pedestrian and stops less predictably. The legal position is also clear: private e-scooters are illegal on public roads and pavements in many UK areas, yet enforcement is weak. A ban would remove ambiguity, protect vulnerable users, and restore the pavement as safe shared space. Safety must outweigh convenience.

The pro side paints a frightening picture, but a blanket ban is disproportionate. Many riders use pavements because roads feel unsafe and cycling infrastructure is incomplete. Banning scooters simply pushes people back into cars, worsening congestion and pollution. Pavement conflict can be managed through design: slower speeds, clearer markings, and better separation. Riders are often commuters trying to make short trips efficiently. Enforcement, education, and local rules would address bad behaviour without removing a useful transport option. We should target dangerous riders, not the technology itself. A ban would punish responsible users for the actions of a few.

The con side says design and education will fix the problem, but it offers no evidence that such measures actually reduce injuries. Voluntary slow-down schemes have failed where they exist, because riders ignore them. The claim that bans push people into cars is speculative; many e-scooter trips replace walking or short public transport legs, not car journeys. Saying we should target dangerous riders ignores that pavement use itself is the danger. When a pedestrian is hit, intent does not matter. A clear ban is enforceable, predictable, and protects the most vulnerable.

The pro side keeps returning to fear, but the real question is how we manage shared space sensibly. Many cities have found that clear rules, consistent messaging, and visible local enforcement change behaviour quickly. A ban would be difficult to apply and would drive riding underground, making conflicts harder to track. It would also hit people who rely on scooters for independence. We can set speed limits, create shared zones, and prioritise pedestrian space without removing scooters entirely. The answer is regulation and good design, not prohibition.

The con side still has not shown that regulation works in practice, nor given a single concrete example of a scheme that reduced pavement injuries. Its answer to every problem is more rules, but rules without evidence are just hope. Meanwhile, real pedestrians suffer real injuries. A ban is simple, visible, and enforceable. It removes a clear conflict between vehicles and vulnerable pavement users. It also signals that pavements are for people first. The burden of proof lies with those who want scooters on pavements, and that burden has not been met. We should ban them.

The pro side wants to ban a useful form of transport because of a problem that can be managed. We believe in targeted rules, better infrastructure, and local flexibility, not blanket prohibition. A ban would be blunt, unpopular, and hard to sustain. It would ignore the needs of riders and the realities of urban streets. The better path is clear standards, consistent enforcement, and design that separates people from vehicles where needed. Let us keep scooters but manage them sensibly. That is a balanced, practical response, and it deserves your support.

motion: Exams should be replaced by continuous assessment.

transcript.motion: Exams should be replaced by continuous assessment.

turns.text: Exams are a high-stakes lottery, not a measure of learning. A 2023 Stanford study found that a single three-hour test explains less than 40 percent of variance in final grades. Continuous assessment, by contrast, samples performance across the whole term. In Finland, where exam pressure is low and coursework is continuous, student well-being scores are 30 percent higher than the OECD average. Replacing exams with portfolios, projects and periodic quizzes would reduce anxiety, reward consistent effort, and give teachers feedback they can actually act on. We should judge students on their sustained work, not their worst day.

The pro side paints exams as cruel, but the real cruelty is lowering standards. Final exams have been the backbone of serious education for centuries, and for good reason. They create a shared deadline that forces students to integrate knowledge, not just skim it. If we abolish them, we drift into a world where a student can coast on small tasks and never face a real challenge. You either test what students know at the end, or you surrender to a soft, fragmented system. There is no serious middle ground, and tradition here is not superstition but hard-won wisdom.

My opponent calls this a drift, but that is a slippery slope with no evidence. Continuous assessment does not mean no standards; it means more data points. In New Zealand, which replaced high-stakes exams with standards-based coursework, university retention rose by 12 percent. Their students still face deadlines, moderation and external checks. The false choice between a single exam and no challenge ignores the reality that coursework can be rigorous. We are not surrendering standards; we are spreading them across the term so one bad night cannot erase ten weeks of work.

The pro side cites New Zealand, but their system works because of small classes and heavy funding, not because exams vanished. Copying it elsewhere is wishful thinking. More fundamentally, the proposal attacks the wrong problem. If students are anxious, the answer is better teaching and support, not dismantling the one tool that forces everyone to prove their knowledge at the same moment. My opponents are experienced teachers, but experience has not stopped them from ignoring how real workplaces operate: deadlines, pressure, and a final product. We should not redesign education around comfort.

Let me be clear: the evidence favors continuous assessment. It reduces the luck of a single day, matches how modern workplaces actually evaluate people, and gives teachers actionable feedback. The con side has argued that exams must survive because they always have, and that removing them leads to a soft system. Both claims are fallacies. Tradition is not proof, and there is no evidence that coursework lowers standards. In fact, moderation and external review can make it stricter. We are not choosing comfort over rigor; we are choosing a fairer, more accurate system. Vote pro.

The pro side wants you to believe that because some systems use coursework, all exams are obsolete. That is a leap. Exams remain the clearest, fairest way to verify that a student can perform without help, on demand, against a common standard. Continuous assessment may be kinder, but kindness is not the same as rigor. If we abandon the final test, we risk a generation that can complete tasks but cannot think under pressure. The motion asks us to replace, not refine. For that reason, I urge you to reject it and keep exams.

motion: Restaurants should show calorie counts on menus.

transcript.motion: Restaurants should show calorie counts on menus.

turns.text: Calorie information empowers diners to make informed choices at the point of purchase. When people see that a burger contains over a thousand calories, many choose a lighter option without being told what to do. Several cities already require this, and evaluations show modest reductions in calories purchased. Transparency respects consumer autonomy and supports public health goals, especially as portion sizes have grown. It also encourages restaurants to reformulate dishes to avoid looking excessive. In short, posting calories is a light-touch policy that nudges better decisions while leaving freedom intact.

The evidence does not support the promise. A large New York University study after labeling began found no meaningful change in calories purchased, and some people ordered more. Labels impose real costs on small restaurants: lab analysis, menu reprints, and constant updates for seasonal ingredients. They also mislead, since actual calories can vary by twenty percent or more with preparation. Worst of all, they can harm people with eating disorders, for whom numbers on a menu are a trigger, not information. A policy that fails to change behavior while burdening businesses and endangering vulnerable diners is hard to defend.

The core principle remains transparency. Calorie labels give people knowledge they say they want; surveys consistently show most diners favor having the information available. Even modest shifts matter at population scale, and labels push restaurants toward healthier recipes over time. The policy is simple, visible where decisions happen, and preserves choice rather than restricting it. As chains standardize recipes, accuracy improves. Informing consumers is a legitimate goal, and posting calories is a practical, low-cost step toward a more honest food environment where people can align purchases with their own health goals.

My opponents repeat the transparency claim, but the question is whether it works, and the studies say it does not. The NYU evaluation I cited directly answers their 'modest shifts' assertion: calories purchased were statistically unchanged. Support in surveys also ignores behavior; people say they want labels yet rarely use them. Their 'low-cost' framing contradicts the compliance burden on independent kitchens. And they never address the eating-disorder risk, which turns their 'knowledge' into harm for a vulnerable group. Repeating the same point does not fix absent evidence, real costs, or serious downside.

In closing, calorie labels are a modest, reasonable measure that arms consumers with information and encourages better industry norms. People deserve to know what is in their food, and posting counts does so without bans or taxes. Cities with rules show it is administrable, and menus can be designed cleanly. Over time, visibility nudges both diners and kitchens toward lighter, healthier options. The principle of informed choice is sound, the policy is practical, and the public-health logic is clear. We urge you to support transparency on menus.

Their closing again ignores the evidence: no significant behavior change, real costs for small restaurants, unreliable numbers, and documented harm to those with eating disorders. 'Informed choice' sounds good, but if labels do not change intake, they only add expense and risk. The studies they never answer stand. Surveys about wanting information do not equal healthier outcomes, and menu redesign cannot fix a failed nudge. A policy that burdens businesses, misleads customers, and endangers vulnerable people should fail. I urge you to reject the motion.

motion: Children under 13 should not have social media accounts.

transcript.motion: Children under 13 should not have social media accounts.

turns.text: We support the motion because developing brains are uniquely vulnerable. A 2023 Surgeon General advisory found that adolescents who spend more than three hours a day on social media double their risk of anxiety and depression symptoms. Platforms designed for adults use infinite scroll and likes that exploit reward pathways; children under 13 lack the prefrontal maturity to resist. The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act already recognizes this by restricting data collection under 13, yet enforcement is patchy. A clear age floor would end the current chaos where nine-year-olds lie about birthdays. Protecting children from addictive design is not censorship; it is basic public health policy.

We oppose the motion because blanket bans ignore the real benefits of connection and learning. Many young people use platforms to stay close to family, explore creative interests, and find community when local options are limited. A strict cutoff pushes usage underground, making it less visible to parents and educators who could guide it. Rather than prohibiting access, we should focus on building skills, encouraging open dialogue, and involving families. Children develop at different rates, so rigid age rules are clumsy tools. Trusting responsible use and support works far better than turning an everyday activity into a forbidden thrill.

The con side says bans push usage underground, but current law already fails, with studies showing roughly half of parents of tweens report their child has an account despite rules. Underground use means children face harmful content alone, not with guidance. Con claims connection benefits, yet a 2024 longitudinal study linked earlier account creation to worse sleep and higher distress, not stronger friendships. We cannot teach restraint in an environment engineered by behavioral scientists to bypass it. The only way to keep preteens safe from manipulative design is to deny them access until they have the cognitive tools to resist it.

Pro frames this as a simple safety switch, but prohibition rarely produces safety in practice. Families who talk openly and set shared expectations achieve better outcomes than those relying on hard cutoffs that invite secrecy. Children need practice navigating digital spaces before they leave home, and a total ban removes that rehearsal. We also risk widening gaps, since resourceful families will find workarounds while others lose access to helpful communities. Instead of focusing on age gates, we should promote media literacy, compassionate supervision, and platform accountability. Real protection comes from engaged adults, not from pretending a line on a calendar solves everything.

In closing, the evidence is clear: platforms built for adult engagement harm children. The Surgeon General advisory, COPPA’s own logic, and repeated studies show early exposure predicts worse mental health, not better connection. Con asks us to trust guidance, yet guidance cannot compete with algorithms optimized to hold attention. Con worries about secrecy, but secrecy already flourishes under today’s weak enforcement; a firm standard would give schools and parents clarity, not confusion. We do not let children buy alcohol because some families might supervise it. Similarly, an under-13 limit is a necessary, evidence-based protection. We urge you to support the motion.

In closing, we believe the goal is healthy, capable children, not excluded ones. A hard cutoff treats every young person as equally at risk and ignores the real support that families, mentors, and educators can provide. When we focus on conversation, skill-building, and sensible boundaries, children learn to manage technology rather than fear it. Blanket bans drive behavior out of sight, widen inequalities, and remove opportunities for belonging and creativity. We should hold platforms accountable and empower adults, not remove tools from young lives. A thoughtful, inclusive approach protects far more children than a simple prohibition ever could.

motion: Gap years before university are worthwhile.

transcript.motion: Gap years before university are worthwhile.

turns.text: For centuries, young people have paused before serious study, and societies that preserved this rite of passage produced thoughtful citizens. A gap year lets students mature, travel, and return with purpose. Those who dismiss it simply never stepped outside a classroom themselves. We should trust the wisdom of generations over fleeting trends. Without this breathing space, students are forced straight into pressure, losing the chance to discover who they are. Tradition endures because it works, and a year of real-world experience naturally creates sharper, more motivated learners than any uninterrupted conveyor belt ever could.

The evidence points the other way. A 2018 study by the National Student Clearinghouse found that students who delayed enrollment were far less likely to complete a degree within six years. In Germany, where gap years are common, tracking data show longer delays often become permanent detours, especially for first-generation students. Work, travel, and caregiving easily slip into drifting. Financially, a lost year means lost earnings and extra tuition inflation. Rather than a magical rite of passage, a gap year is a risky pause that advantages the already privileged and quietly pushes others out of higher education.

My opponent cites statistics, but the real issue is motivation. Students who choose a gap year are self-selected; they return hungrier and more focused. If some drift, that reflects poor planning, not the idea itself. Notice who argues against this: administrators who profit from full lecture halls and never left home themselves. Their fear of change should not outweigh lived experience. Besides, the claim that one year derails a life ignores countless graduates who flourished after time abroad. We should not let spreadsheets erase what every mature student knows: perspective gained outside school deepens learning inside it.

Self-selection explains why raw comparisons flatter gap years. When researchers control for family income and prior achievement, the completion gap remains. Calling critics names does not change the German finding that delays hurt first-generation applicants most. Nor does 'perspective' answer the student who loses a scholarship, a visa, or a rented room. Structured internships help, but they are not what most take. My opponent defends a pause as if it were a cure, yet the data show it behaves like a tax on ambition. Motivation matters, but so does staying on the ladder long enough to climb.

In closing, remember that the greatest harm is a generation rushed into degrees without direction. Universities admit more anxious, uncertain students every year, and a gap year offers relief. Those who warn of risk forget that risk exists everywhere; staying on a conveyor belt can be the biggest gamble of all. We should honor the young adult who pauses to work, volunteer, or travel, and returns with stories that animate seminars. A year outside the classroom is not lost time. It is the foundation that makes every later lecture meaningful, and that alone justifies the motion.

The pro side never answered the core finding: delay predicts non-completion, especially for students without family wealth. Calling a gap year a foundation does not make it one when scholarships lapse, skills rust, and peers graduate ahead. Tradition and anecdotes are not evidence, and attacking administrators does not repair a broken timeline. If a pause were truly worthwhile, we would see equal gains across income groups, yet we see the opposite. Support students with paid internships, advising, and bridge programs instead. The motion romanticizes a year that, for many, quietly ends a dream. I urge you to reject it.

motion: Shops should not open on public holidays.

transcript.motion: Shops should not open on public holidays.

turns.text: Public holidays exist to protect rest, family time and shared civic meaning, yet mandatory shop openings erode all three. In Germany, the Federal Labour Ministry found that employees in retail report 30 percent higher stress levels during holiday trading weeks. A 2022 British Retail Consortium survey showed nearly half of shop workers wanted holidays off, even at the cost of bonus pay. When shops stay open, families fragment, community events lose attendance and low-wage staff bear the burden. Closing shops for a handful of days each year restores a minimal collective pause, benefiting mental health, children and local neighbourhoods far more than marginal extra sales.

The con side believes shops should remain open because consumers and workers both gain. Extended hours create flexible part-time shifts for students, carers and people who prefer holiday premiums. In Australia, the 2017 Easter trading reforms in New South Wales lifted small-business revenue by around 12 percent, helping independent stores survive. Shoppers with irregular schedules rely on holiday access for essentials, gifts and travel needs. Voluntary opt-in contracts let willing staff earn extra while others rest, respecting individual choice. Instead of blanket bans, sensible regulation, fair pay and rotation systems protect employees while preserving service, tourism revenue and modern family routines that no longer fit a single shared day off.

The con side praises choice, but the evidence shows it is mostly illusory. When a 2021 UK government pilot let councils opt into Sunday trading, staff surveys still reported pressure to accept shifts or risk hours. The Australian revenue gain cited ignores that much came from displaced spending from nearby towns, not new demand. Meanwhile, the core harm stands: public holidays are precisely when children, parents and overworked staff most need time together. If flexibility matters, it should be delivered through predictable rosters on normal days, not by converting every symbolic rest day into a trading day that shifts costs onto the lowest-paid workers.

Our position remains grounded in practical benefits for real households. Holiday trading supports vulnerable workers who need extra income, students fitting study around shifts, and parents who use premium pay for childcare. Retail access also helps tourists, shift workers and people whose religious or cultural days differ from the majority calendar. The New South Wales reforms demonstrate that well-designed rules can boost small firms without harming staff, especially when paired with penalties, rest breaks and voluntary rosters. Blanket closure is a blunt instrument in a diverse society. Flexible employment, higher wages and consumer convenience offer a fairer, more modern balance than rigid bans imposed on everyone.

In closing, the pro side asks for a small, clear boundary: a few days when commerce pauses so community life can breathe. The con side has not shown that holiday openings create genuine freedom; they mainly transfer time from poorly paid staff to convenience-driven consumption. Studies from Germany, Britain and Australia all point to higher stress, displaced demand and weak gains. Public holidays are not ordinary trading days; they anchor memory, family rituals and mental recovery. Protecting them costs little yet yields broad social benefits. The motion therefore deserves support, because a society that never stops shopping also never truly rests, never truly gathers, and never fully honours its workers.

In closing, the con side reaffirms that open shops serve diverse modern lives. Holiday trading gives students, carers and low-income staff access to higher-paid voluntary work, helps small businesses survive seasonal shocks, and lets shoppers buy essentials when they need them. With fair penalties, rotation and rest rules, workers are protected without stripping everyone of choice. Tourism, local economies and families with non-standard schedules all benefit from flexible hours. Rather than imposing one rigid calendar, policy should trust negotiated agreements, decent pay and sensible regulation. That approach respects pluralism, supports employment and keeps essential services available, which is why we urge you to reject the motion.

motion: Printed newspapers will disappear within twenty years.

transcript.motion: Printed newspapers will disappear within twenty years.

turns.text: The direction of travel is unmistakable. Readers, especially younger ones, expect news that is instant, searchable, and free, and advertisers follow those readers wherever they go. Printing presses, delivery trucks, and bundles of paper are simply too slow and too costly for a world that now consumes information through glass screens. As subscriptions and single-copy sales keep sliding, editors will move their reporting online, and the physical product will quietly fade, first in big cities and then everywhere. Twenty years is more than enough time for a habit built over centuries to break, once the economics no longer support it.

The evidence points to adaptation, not extinction. In the United States, weekday print circulation was still about 20 million in 2022, according to Pew Research, and many papers like The New York Times now hold more digital subscribers than print ones while keeping a profitable Sunday edition. In Japan, the Yomiuri Shimbun prints more than six million copies a day. A 2023 Reuters Institute report found that even in digitally advanced markets, roughly a third of people still use print news at least occasionally. Print offers focused reading, local reach, and ad formats that still command premium prices, so it will shrink but persist.

Those numbers describe a long, slow slide, not survival. A product that keeps losing readers year after year, that struggles to attract young subscribers, and that depends on an ageing audience is already living on borrowed time. Once the most loyal readers begin to drop off, the economics of printing, distributing, and selling papers will unravel quickly. Editors will not wait for the last reader to leave; they will shift budgets to digital formats where growth and data are stronger. The remaining copies will look like nostalgic editions, not a durable business model capable of lasting another two decades.

You describe decline, but decline is not disappearance. The New York Times Company reported more than ten million total subscribers in 2023, with print still contributing substantial revenue through high-margin Sunday editions and bundled pricing. In Germany, Bild am Sonntag and Bild print millions of copies weekly, even as digital grows, because print readers over-index on local and weekend habits. Your argument about ageing audiences ignores loyalty: older readers stay longer than expected, and some younger readers return to print for focused time. The trend is contraction and consolidation, not extinction, and twenty years is too short to erase a deeply embedded, still-profitable format.

The core question is whether any new generation will form the habit of reading a folded paper over coffee. That habit is already rare among the young, who treat news as a stream they can skim, share, and discuss online. As costs rise and revenues fall, papers will cut frequency, shrink pages, and finally stop printing altogether, keeping their journalism alive on screens. History shows that when a physical medium loses its everyday use, it does not linger for long. The final editions will not be dramatic, just quiet, as publishers choose the cheaper, faster, more measurable path of digital distribution.

The pro side offers a story about habits, but the record shows resilience. In the UK, The Daily Mail’s print circulation remained above one million in 2023, while MailOnline grew, proving the two can reinforce each other. The motion demands complete disappearance within twenty years, and the evidence from multiple countries, from subscriber data to ongoing ad demand, simply does not support that absolute claim.
